among Russian cities in terms of industrial output. In St. Petersburg,
there are more than 740 large and medium-sized industrial companies
involved in virtually all types of industrial work ( CPPI, 2016). In addi-

trade port in the Russian Federation, accommodates intensive trafﬁco f
cargo and passenger ships ( Kotikov, 2015; BPO, 2017). Together with
the high level of air pollution, the deterioration processes of the mate-
rials also largely depend on unfavourable climatic conditions, especially
the high relative humidity (78% as annual average) which ampliﬁes the
anthropogenic impact on materials. The effects of the environment on
the cultural heritage of St. Petersburg and the degradation processes
of stone and bronze monuments have been extensively studied
(Frank-Kamenetskaya et al., 2009 ; Vlasov et al., 2019 ; Frank-
Kamenetskaya et al., 2019).
Although most air pollution problems in European cities are caused
by local sources of emissions, an important part of the pollution origi-
nates from the regional background or from transboundaryﬂows of pol-
lutants generated in other countries (CLRTAP, 2016). For instance, four
Greek UNESCO sites located on islands in the Aegean Sea ( Medieval
City of Rhodes , Pythagoreion and Heraion of Samos , The Historic Centre
(Chorá) with the Monastery of Saint-John the Theologian and the Cave of
the Apocalypse on the Island of Pátmosand Delos) display substantial po-
tential damage to materials although there is no large local pollution
source. These islands are among the most popular cruise destinations
in Greece. Vehicular emissions were found to be major contributor to
the ambient concentrations of PM 10 in Rhodes ( Argyropoulos et al.,
2012). In addition, several Greek islands are not connected to the
main electricity grid and most of them satisfy their power requirements
using oil-fuelled power plants. The demand is very high especially dur-
ing the summer months due to their status as popular tourist destina-
tions ( Chalakatevaki et al., 2017 ). A study on the weathering
mechanisms of marbles and granites used in the monuments of Delos
(Chabas and Lefèvre, 2000) highlighted two atmospheric sources able
to participate in the deterioration of the archaeological site: an impor-
tant natural source of marine salts and an anthropic source which indi-
cates pollution at a regional (Aegean maritime traf ﬁc) and remote
(Black Sea and Bosphorus areas) scales.
4. Conclusions
In this study, several corrosion maps for different materials and a
soiling map for Europe were obtained by applying available dose-
response functions and using environmental data from a well recog-
nized chemical transport atmospheric model as input. In general, the re-
sults indicate that, despite of a signi ﬁcant decrease of air pollution in
Europe over the past few decades, air pollution is still considerable
and continues to be an important agent of degradation of materials.
In a subsequent step, the corrosion and soiling maps were overlaid
with the UNESCO cultural sites map in order to have an answer to the
second objective of the study: estimate the current potential impacts
of air pollution on materials of cultural objects, taking the UNESCO
World Cultural Heritage sites as the case study. The potential risk was
estimated on the basis of exceeding tolerable degradation thresholds
suggested for each material. The resulting picture indicates that a fair
number of sites are exposed to high concentrations of air pollutants
and consequently they can suffer damage. In general, metropolitan
areas are the environments in which air pollutants can be present at
high levels and can therefore directly affect the materials of cultural
heritage.
Although the methodology used in this study provides a simpli ﬁed
assessment of the likelihood of damage to UNESCO's cultural heritage
in Europe from air pollution, it provides a unique perspective and the
potential risk is assessed on a common basis. The results obtained con-
tribute to a better understanding of the existing potential risk deriving
from atmospheric pollution and to highlighting the sites that need par-
ticular attention, generally located in areas where anthropogenic activ-
ity is relevant. The present paper can serve as a basis for stimulating
additional studies and site-speci ﬁc analyzes, as well as highlighting
the need for further measures and policies for atmospheric pollution re-
duction in cities and in the surroundings of sensitive historic buildings
and monuments to prevent further damage.

In many modern cities, the manufacturing sector has been overtaken
by the services sector, though it remains important. Some of the cities
that are home to the UNESCO properties that seem at risk from air pol-
lution according to Table 3 are heavily industrialized. Hamburg, Ant-
werp, Ijmuiden (the city close to the Coastal Fort of the Defence Line
of Amsterdam), Marseille, Dunkerque, Tarragona, the areas which lie
to the north of Oviedo, the Gulf of Vizcaya, Istanbul, Bursa, the Upper Si-
lesia region, the North of Italy, Ravenna, Syracuse, and others areas and
European cities have intense industrial activities (petrochemical, chem-
istry, steel, non-ferrous metals, cement plant, power plants including
coal-ﬁred power plants, etc.). Even areas that at ﬁrst glance may seem
scarcely affected by human impact can suffer from air pollution, such
as the Gorham's Cave Complex in Gibraltar, a British Overseas Territory
located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. According to the
EEA database, Gibraltar has among the worst air quality in any UK terri-
tory. Within a radius of a few kilometres from the centre of Gibraltar, to
the north and west there is an intensively industrialized area on the
Spanish coast. This includes the largest oil reﬁnery in the Iberian Penin-
sula, manufacturers of re ﬁned petroleum products and organic basic
chemicals, several power plants (included a coal- ﬁred power plant)
and a steel producer ( Pandolﬁ et al., 2011 ; Fauser et al., 2013 ). The
Port of Gibraltar is one of the Mediterranean's biggest bunkering ports
and also an attractive and popular tourist destination. The port of Alge-
ciras on the Spanish coast is the second port of Spain and third in the
Mediterranean Sea. In 2017 more than 100,000 vessels passed through
the Strait of Gibraltar.
A signiﬁcant number of UNESCO sites at risk of damage due to air
pollution are located in Italy. This is not only because Italy is the
European country with the highest number of sites in the WHL but
also because the country has among the worst air pollution in all of
Europe. Italy has one of the highest motorization rates in Europe, with
an average of 625 cars per 1000 inhabitants, compared to 562 cars per
1000 residents in Germany, 479 in France and 472 in UK ( UNECE,
2020). Not surprisingly, a number of cities with the most polluted air
are located in northern Italy, one of the most anthropized and populated
areas in Europe. The Po valley is surrounded by the Alps to the North
and North-West and by the Apennines to the South. The occurrence of
low-wind periods and atmospheric stability conditions favour the accu-
mulation of pollutants locally emitted. The high pressure of industrial
and agricultural activities, the high road traf ﬁc and the relatively cold
winter temperatures that favour prolonged and intensive use of domes-
tic heating during the cold months determine pollution levels above the
limit set by the European Air Quality Directive and by the World Health
Organization (ISPRA, 2020). Due to the intense solar radiation in sum-
mer, high levels of ozone are produced in Italy.

2. Materials and methods
Properties inscribed in the 2017 UNESCO World Heritage List
(http://whc.unesco.org/en/list/) were considered in the present study.
Data (geographical position, property and buffer boundaries, etc.) for
cultural sites falling in the geographical scope of the present study (geo-
graphic area between 30°N-82°N latitude and 30°W-47°E longitude, ex-
cluding North Africa and the Middle East) was retrieved. As a number of
sites, including transboundary and transnational sites, are characterized
by multiple locations, 1276 cells of the studied domain where at least
one cultural object of the World Heritage List (WHL) is located have
been identiﬁed. All cultural sites were mapped in a common geographic
coordinate system (WGS84). The spatial distribution of the cells hosting
the cultural objects is shown in Fig. 1.
Data at ground level on air pollution and meteorology were re-
trieved from the EMEP/MSC-W database ( https://emep.int/mscw/
mscw_moddata.html) for the year 2015 at a resolution of 0.1° × 0.1°
longitude-latitude. This resolution corresponds to sizes of grid cell of
6 × 11 km at 60°N and 9 × 11 km at 40°N. Data include the average an-
nual concentrations of SO 2,N O 2, HNO 3,O 3,a n dP M10 (particles with
aerodynamic diameter less than 10 μm), annual averages of tempera-
ture and relative humidity as well as the total annual precipitation. pH
of rainwater was not available in the EMEP/MSC-W database. pH values
from approximately 200 sites, including stations of the EMEP monitor-
ing network, were interpolated according to the Inverse Distance
Weighting (IDW) algorithm. An output raster layer at a resolution of
0.1° × 0.1° longitude-latitude was produced.
The currently of ﬁcial dose-response functions, ﬁrst year exposure,
for a range of materials have been applied to link pollutant concentra-
tions and meteorological variables with the predicted damage rate of
the different materials. Table 1 lists the dose-response functions used
in this study and the explanation of the related parameters. All of
them are based on the results obtained in the ICP Materials exposure
programme (Tidblad et al., 2001; Kucera et al., 2007)a n dt h eE Up r o j e c t
MULTI-ASSESS (Kucera, 2005). Two sets of dose-response functions are
available for the corrosion of materials due to air pollution: functions for
the SO2 dominating scenario and functions for a multi-pollutant sce-
nario. In the present study, dose-response functions for the multi-
pollutant scenario were used to predict corrosion rates for limestone,
copper, bronze, carbon steel and zinc. For sandstone, only the function
for the SO2 dominating scenario was available.
The dose-response functions use the annual averages of the values of
the concentrations of air pollutants and climatic parameters as input
data and return the average annual values of corrosion. The metric of
corrosion rates is surface recession or corrosion depth, (R, μm), which
can be de ﬁned as the displacement of a point on the corroded surface
of the material with respect to its initial position on the non-corroded
surface taken as the reference point. Corrosion rates are also expressed
in terms of mass loss (g m −2). Mass losses can be converted into R by
dividing ML by the density of the material (g cm−3). Soiling of modern
glass, expressed as haze, was estimated according to a dose-response
function based on a multi-linear regression equation reported by
Lombardo et al. (2010).
The surface corrosion or soiling for all materials was calculated for
each cell of the studied domain by applying the relevant dose-
response function with the available data on modelled concentrations
of air pollutants and meteorological parameters. Corrosion maps and
soiling maps for every selected material were derived. All the spatial
representation and interpolation methodologies have been performed
using the Open Source Geographic Information System QGIS 2.18 soft-
ware (QGIS, 2018). The corrosion rate or soiling values were extracted
from the layer according to the monument's geographic location and
examined in order to evaluate the potential risk to air pollution of
UNESCO WHL sites. Targets for the protection of infrastructure materials
and cultural heritage monuments have been suggested by ICP Materials
as a multiple (n) of the background corrosion rate. These have been set
at n = 2.5 for the year 2020 and n = 2 for 2050 ( ECE, 2009; CLRTAP,
2014). The tolerable degradation rates adopted in the present study
are reported in Table 2. No target has been proposed until now for the
soiling of glass artefacts. Consequently, in the following sections the
soiling of modern glass will be discussed but no quantitative evaluation
will be carried out on the potential damage.

hand and the resulting rate of material degradation on the other. By
mapping the areas where important sites and monuments are located,
it is possible to quantitatively analyze the risk of damage and identify
the areas most at risk for the different materials. This method can be a
useful tool for the authorities in charge of managing sites of cultural in-
terest and for policy makers in developing strategies to reduce air pollu-
tion for the sustainable maintenance and reduced damage to cultural
heritage.
Several studies of the mapping of areas with cultural heritage objects
are available in the literature on different geographical scales, ranging
from cities such as Madrid ( de la Fuente et al., 2011 ; de la Fuente
et al., 2013 ), Istanbul ( Karaca, 2013 ), and Mexico City ( Castillo-
Miranda et al., 2017 ), countries such as Italy ( De Marco et al., 2017 ),
and regions like Europe ( Di Turo et al., 2016 ). Although these studies
differ in several details, a fairly coherent overall picture emerges. The
degradation rate of materials of cultural heritage objects has decreased
over the last decades thanks to the implementation of measures and
policies for the control of air pollution. However, they show that there
are still exceedances of tolerable degradation of cultural heritage
materials.
The present study has two main purposes. Theﬁrst is the generation
of corrosion and soling maps for different materials that can be useful
for predicting the damage due to air pollution in Europe. The second
aims at analysing the current potential impacts of air pollution on mate-
rials of cultural objects, taking the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage sites
as the case study. Corrosion and soiling maps were obtained using the
dose-response functions developed by the International Co-operative
Programme on Effects on Materials including Historic and Cultural
Monuments (ICP Materials). Yearly gridded data of input parameters
for calculating degradation rates were taken from the output of the
EMEP/MSC-W model on the 0.1° × 0.1° longitude-latitude grid.
Properties nominated for World Heritage status have their values
assessed according to UNESCO's natural and cultural criteria, which
are explained in the Operational Guidelines for the Implementation of
the World Heritage Convention ( UNESCO, 2019 ). According to
UNESCO ( https://whc.unesco.org/en/factors/ ), air pollution arising
from industrialization and uncontrolled urbanization is one of the
threats/factors affecting the Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) of
World Heritage properties.
ICP Materials (www.corr-institute.se/icp-materials) started in 1985,
together with other International Cooperative Programmes (ICPs) on
effects on ecosystems, health and crops, to support the Convention on
Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP) ( http://www.
unece.org/env/lrtap/welcome.html.html ), within the United Nations
Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE). Data collected during the
ICP Materials ﬁeld exposure programme, together with those produced
in other projects such as MULTI-ASSESS (Kucera, 2005), allowed the de-
velopment of empirical dose-response functions. These functions de-
scribe the quantitative relationship between the dose, given by the air
pollution concentration in combination with climatic parameters, and
the response, expressed as either material mass loss (expressed in g
m−2) or surface recession (loss in thickness, expressed in μm) for sev-
eral materials (Tidblad et al., 2001; Kucera et al., 2007; CLRTAP, 2014).
The Cooperative Programme for Monitoring and Evaluation of the
Long-range Transmission of Air Pollutants in Europe (EMEP) has oper-
ated under the CLRTAP since 1983. The EMEP model ( Simpson et al.,
2012), developed by the Meteorological Synthesizing Centre-West of
EMEP (MSC-W) hosted by the Norwegian Meteorological Institute, is
one of the key tools for the development of air quality polices in the
European Union. Modelled air concentration and deposition data can
be downloaded (https://emep.int/mscw/mscw_moddata.html)a s ﬁles
that cover the EMEP grid. The resolution of the grid has changed over

(IPCC, 2018), with consequent economic and social costs ( EEA, 2011;
WHO/OECD, 2015 ; WBG, 2016 ; Dechezleprêtre et al., 2019 ). Atmo-
spheric pollution is also a major factor for the degradation of materials
which are components of structures and buildings of civil engineering
(Leygraf et al., 2016 ), leading to economic losses due to high mainte-
nance, repair, renovation and cleaning costs ( Newby et al., 1991 ;
Cowell and Apsimon, 1996 ; Rabl, 1999 ; Watt et al., 2009 ). A non-
quantiﬁable value, which goes well beyond the economic losses of the
deteriorated material, is added when these materials are part of histor-
ical and cultural monuments.
Natural weathering of materials exposed outdoor is a process deter-
mined by the effect of factors such as thermal variations, sunlight, wind,
rain, humidity, crystallization of soluble salts, growth of microorganism
colonies, growth of superior plants, etc. Atmospheric pollutants act as
intensifying and accelerating factors of the natural aging processes of
materials (Groysman, 2010; Camuffo, 2016). The more aggressive pol-
lutants for the deterioration processes of materials of historic buildings
and monuments are carbon dioxide (CO2), sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitro-
gen oxides (NOx), ozone (O3), and atmospheric particles (PM).
CO2 is not considered a pollutant in itself, but a climate-altering gas.
However, CO 2 from the air dissolves in rainwater making it slightly
acidic (carbonic acid, H 2CO3). The rainwater may react with materials
that are largely made from calcium carbonates (CaCO 3) – limestone
being a common example - transforming the calcium carbonate, slightly
soluble, into the more soluble calcium bicarbonate (Ca(HCO3)2). This is
washed away causing the material to be weathered, the so-called karst
effect (Lipfert, 1989).
SO2 originates predominantly from the combustion of sulphur-
containing fossil fuels and the smelting of sulphide ores. Sulphur diox-
ide has long been recognized as one of the most critical atmospheric
pollutants for stone materials. SO2 reacts with calcium carbonate (cal-
cite) producing gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O). During formation of the degra-
dation layers of gypsum, the particulate emitted fromﬁxed and mobile
combustion sources is incorporated into the mineral matrix. Visually,
these changes appear in the form of blackened surfaces (black crusts),
particularly where the stone is sheltered from rain and protected from
intensive wash-out. Eventually the black crusts blister andﬂake, causing
the detachment of the crusts and loss of material (Amoroso and Fassina,
1983; Camuffo et al., 1983; Moropoulou et al., 1998; Ausset et al., 1999).
SO2 has also been recognized as an important factor in the corrosion of
many metals such as steel, zinc, aluminium, copper, and bronze, often in
combination with other pollutants ( Oesch and Faller, 1997 ; Tidblad,
2016).
Anthropogenic NO x are formed in combustion processes at high
temperatures during the operation of motor vehicles and various indus-
trial activities. During the fuel burning, nitrogen monoxide (NO) is
formed ﬁrst, which is further oxidized to dioxide (NO 2). The main
source for NO 2 in urban air is automotive exhausts. NO and NO 2,t o -
gether with atmospheric oxygen and hydrocarbons, are involved in a
cycle that leads to the generation of ozone (Stephens, 1969), act as pre-
cursors of nitrate aerosol, and contribute to regional radiation forcing
(Molina and Molina, 2004; Seinfeld and Pandis, 2016). Ozone is respon-
sible for most of the oxidizing power of the smog atmosphere and exerts
a role in the degradation of metals such as copper and copper alloys and
in the oxidation of polymeric materials such as rubber.
The oxidation products of SO2 and NOx, sulphuric acid (H2SO4)a n d
nitric acid (HNO3), have been recognized as important factors in the de-
terioration of materials. Natural precipitation, rain and snow, is slightly
acidic due to the dissolution of CO2 and pH in natural rainwater is about
5.6. Acidic aerosols lead to an increased acidity of rain and snow. In the
past, this phenomenon was particularly important in Nordic countries,
with heavy impacts on vegetation and aquatic environment ( Likens,
1976). The increased acidity enhances the weathering and corrosion
of materials and buildings, too (Camuffo, 1992; Livingston, 2016).
Atmospheric particulate matter (PM) can be directly emitted by var-
ious stationary and mobile sources, mainly as a product of combustion
of fossil fuels (primary emissions), or formed in the atmosphere by
transformation of gaseous emissions (secondary emissions). Secondary
particulate matter precursors include SO 2,N Ox and ammonia (NH 3).
The deposition of airborne particulate matter on surfaces exposed to
the outdoor environment plays an important role in the degradation
process. They are the main cause of the blackening (soiling) that takes
place on surfaces exposed to the air ( Hamilton and Mans ﬁeld, 1992 ;
Pio et al., 1998 ; Lombardo et al., 2005 ), an effect due in particular to
the carbon particles (soot) originated through the incomplete combus-
tion of fossil fuels. Soiling is very effective in decreasing the aesthetic
value of buildings and monuments ( Grossi and Brimblecombe, 2004).
Soiling of unsheltered surfaces, such as those of buildings or historical
monuments, has an erratic behaviour (Pio et al., 1998). Soiling is depen-
dent on a variety of factors including the type and characteristic of ma-
terial (colour, porosity, surface roughness, etc.), the atmospheric aerosol
characteristics (concentration, size distribution, aerosol colour, etc.), the
type of exposure (orientation of the surface, sheltered or unsheltered
from rainfall, etc.) and the type of climate (windy, humid or dry).
Saline particles are other harmful components for the materials. The
main source for saline particles is the sea salt aerosol. However, chlo-
rides are also present in urban environments, for example due to the
use of salts (sodium and calcium chloride) as de-icing agents on the
roads. The susceptibility of stone materials to salt decay is linked to
the crystallization cycles of the salt into the pore network of the material
and the consequent stress, which gradually weaken the material
(Lubelli, 2006 ). Saline particles also accelerate the metallic corrosion
process (Krätschmer et al., 2002; Knotkova and Kreislova, 2007; Corvo
et al., 2005; Alcántara et al., 2017).
The climatic conditions (temperature, humidity, etc.) contribute
substantially to the degradation rate of materials. In humid, tropical
areas, characterized by permanently high temperatures and high rela-
tive humidity, a high corrosion rate of metals is usually reported
(Tidblad et al., 2000 ; Corvo et al., 2009 ). The Noah's Ark Project
(Sabbioni et al., 2006 ; Brimblecombe et al., 2006 ; Grossi et al., 2007 ;
Bonazza et al., 2009 ; Brimblecombe, 2010 ; Sabbioni et al., 2010 )
highlighted the strong correlation between climate and materials
weathering and focused on the effects of climate change on Europe's
built heritage at different scenarios. There is a general consensus that
air pollutants can act in synergy by signi ﬁcantly increasing the natural
degradation rate of materials while, at the same time, unfavourable cli-
matic parameters can exacerbate the degradation of building materials
caused by pollution.
Atmospheric pollution has drastically decreased in Europe thanks to
targeted environmental policies. The 2019 Report on Air Quality in
Europe (EEA, 2019) indicates that SO 2 have decreased during the last
decades, whereas concentrations of PM and NO2 in 2017 still exceeded
or were very close to the EU limit values in many European regions.
Emissions from motor vehicles and home heating have become the
dominant source of NO2 and PM, in particular in urban agglomerations.
Since many monuments and historic buildings are located in cities, the
possible damage due to corrosion and soiling could be higher there
than in the urban surroundings.
Knowledge of the possible damage to monuments due to air pollu-
tion exposure in the outdoor environment has become an increasingly
important issue in the conservation and protection strategies of cultural
heritage. Continuous monitoring can provide information on the levels
of atmospheric pollutants. However, this methodology has high installa-
tion and maintenance costs and is spatially limited. Remote sensing im-
ages could ﬁll this gap since satellite images cover vast areas. Modelling
of air pollution in urban areas and even more on a regional scale can
provide a spatial representation of pollutant concentrations, allowing
an immediate comparison between different areas. Furthermore, the
scope of investigation can be expanded by producing material damage
maps. This can be done by applying a damage function, a scienti ﬁc
tool that represents the mathematical relationship between the concen-
trations of atmospheric pollutants and climatic parameters on the one

3. Results and discussions
3.1. Limestone
Although composed mainly of calcite (CaCO3), there is a wide variety
of limestone, which can be drastically different not only for aesthetics
but especially in structure and physical properties (density, hardness,
porosity), determining considerable differences in weathering behav-
iour ( Lipfert, 1989 ; Grossi and Murray, 1999 ). The surface recession
map for Portland limestone, obtained applying the multi-pollutant
dose-response function, ﬁrst year exposure (Eq. (1), Table 1) to each
cell of the studied domain is reported in Fig. 2. The limestone recession
rate, ﬁrst year of exposure, appear to be higher across central Europe.
Furthermore, some areas with high recession rates (hotspots) can be
clearly identiﬁed (Russian Federation, North and Central Italy, Turkey,
Balkans).
HNO3 appears to be the most important parameter in determining
current limestone recession rate in most of Europe (Supplementary
data, Fig. S1). SO2, in the past one of the most critical atmospheric pol-
lutants due to its harmful effects on calcareous building stones, at pres-
ent appears relevant only in some areas. PM10 is also an important risk
factor for limestone and its effects seem more relevant in northern Italy,
southern Spain and the westernmost part of Turkey. Rainfall pH seems
to play a role for the surface recession of limestone in Northern
Europe and in some localized areas in Central Europe, Northern Spain
and Northern UK.
3.2. Sandstone
The sandstone varies considerably in consistency and colour, de-
pending on its composition or geographical location of origin. Fig. 3
shows the recession map for white Mans ﬁeld dolomitic sandstone ob-
tained applying the SO 2-dominating dose-response function (Eq. (2),
Table 1). Overall, in most of Europe the recession rate of sandstone ap-
pears low due to low current SO2 concentrations. However, in different
areas the recession rate appears signiﬁcant. These areas are mainly lo-
cated in Iceland (mainly due to volcanic activities), Poland, West
Germany, the Balkan countries, Turkey, Russian Federation and in coun-
tries of Caucasus.
The recession of sandstone is dominated by the presence of SO 2,
while the acidity of precipitation plays a very marginal role except in
the most western areas of the Scandinavian Peninsula (Supplementary
data, Fig. S2). However, it should be emphasized that the dose-
response function used in this study (SO 2-dominating) does not con-
sider other air pollutants such as HNO3 and PM10 which play a very im-
portant role in the recession of limestone. Probably, these pollutants
also exert an effect on sandstone but their contribution cannot be quan-
tiﬁed with the available dose-response function.
3.3. Copper
Architectural copper has been used because of its durability and re-
liability: the copper surface exposed to humidity and the action of the
atmosphere develops a patina as a result of superﬁcial oxidation. Unlike
rust, this patina is pleasing to the eye and protects the underlying cop-
per from further corrosion. The formation and composition of the patina
are signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by the acidity of rain and the atmospheric
pollutants: they dissolve the protective patina on copper accelerating
the corrosion process.
The corrosion map for copper, obtained from Eq. (3), Table 1 ,i s
shown in Fig. 4. Overall, the corrosion rate of copper appears to be sig-
niﬁcant and in vast areas of the domain exceeds the targets set for
2020 (0.8 μm) and 2050 (0.64 μm). The dry deposition, which takes
into account the contributions of SO2 and O3, largely dominates the cor-
rosion of copper artefacts while the wet deposition, expressed by the
amount of precipitation and its hydrogen ion concentration, exercises
a relevant action only in the northernmost European regions (Supple-
mental material, Fig. S3).
3.4. Bronze
Bronze (or bronzes, for the great variety of its possible set of com-
positions) is a material widely used in building structures and for or-
namental purposes in sculptures, monuments and artwork. Bronze
has been preferred for sculpture since antiquity because of its resis-
tance to corrosion and favourable casting properties. Bronze

cated in central Europe, the Balkan Peninsula, Turkey, Iceland and the
Russian Federation, the corrosion rate of bronze appears to be higher
than the targets set for 2020 (0.6 μm, ﬁrst year of exposure) and 2050
(0.5 μm). PM10 seems to be the main responsible for the corrosion of

fair contribution seems to be given by the acidity of the rainfall while
the SO2 plays an important role in some hot spots (Supplemental mate-

3.5. Steel
Cast iron was used for major structures such as bridges, buildings,
monuments and public art objects. Steel (carbon steel and stainless
steel) has been increasingly used to form the structural frames of
multi-storey commercial buildings but also in architectural works.
Hammered wrought iron has been and is still used today for the provi-
sion of decorative elements of buildings. In addition, industrial heritage
sites with their iron and steel equipment constitute an architectural her-
itage documenting the industrial development. Most steels are suscep-
tible to corrosion; alloys such as stainless steel have a higher resistance.
Normally, steel must be protected against corrosion with surface coat-
ings, for example with an organic or metallic covering.
Ferrous materials, due to their wide variety of composition and the
possible presence of protective coatings, have different responses in
terms of susceptibility to atmospheric corrosion. Dose-response func-
tions were derived for carbon steel, weathering steel, coil coated galva-
nized steel with alkyd melamine and steel panels with alkyd ( CLRTAP,
2014). The corrosion map for ferrous materials in the present study
was obtained using the dose-response function for carbon steel in a
multi-pollutant scenario (Eq. (5), Table 1). In most of the studied do-
main the corrosion rate, ﬁrst year of exposure, is not excessively high
(Fig. 6). However, hot spots are evident, in which the corrosion rate ex-
ceeds even the 20 μm target set for 2020. SO 2 still constitutes a domi-
nant factor in the corrosion of the carbon steel. The effect of acidity of
rainfall appears to be signi ﬁcant on the west coast of Scandinavia
while the concentration of PM 10 in the atmosphere generally plays a
minor role (Supplemental material, Fig. S5).
3.6. Zinc
Zinc was extensively used for roo ﬁng in Belgium, Germany and
France, where it replaced more expensive copper and lead. Practically,
all Haussmannian buildings in Paris were covered with zinc and,
today, the classic rooftops of Paris are still over 80% zinc. Zinc castings
are often found into decorative architectural details in building facades
as well as in waterproo ﬁng elements. In Europe, zinc was also cast for
large-scale sculptures starting around 1830. From the mid-1850s
through the early 20th century zinc statues also proliferated in the
United States. The use of zinc for statuary declined after 1900 and
then practically disappeared in the 1950s. Today, many sculptures
made of zinc appear in museum collections but several are still exposed
outdoor.
Fig. 7 shows the corrosion map for zinc (Eq. (6),Table 1). Overall, the
estimated corrosion rate of zinc appears to be signiﬁcant in a large area
of the studied domain, exceeding the target set for 2050 (0.9 μm, ﬁrst
year exposure) and in several hot spots even the target set for 2020
(1.1 μm). The atmospheric concentrations of SO 2 still seem to signi ﬁ-
cantly inﬂuence the corrosion rate of zinc. Also the concentrations of
HNO3 seem to play an important role, particularly in some areas of Cen-
tral Europe, Italy, Greece and Turkey while the pH of precipitation
seems to have some signi ﬁcance only in limited areas of Northern
Europe (Supplemental material, Fig. S6).
3.7. Glass
Glass elements are inseparable architectural components of a his-
toric building. Soda–lime–silica glass is the most prevalent type of mod-
ern glass. Potash-lime-silica glass was predominantly used for stained
glass windows panels in the medieval era. Both types of glass are

eye detects a visual nuisance (Alfaro et al., 2012): the transparent prod-

glass plate is felt.
Fig. 8 shows the spatial variability of glass soiling potential,
expressed in days necessary to reach a haze of 1% and assessed by apply-
ing the dose-response function for the soling of silica–soda–lime mod-
ern glass (Eq. (7), Table 1 ). The map reveals a clear difference
between northern Europe and the central and Mediterranean Europe.
In some parts of northern Italy, south of Spain, in the Balkans, Turkey
and the Russian Federation, high soiling potentials are expected and a
1% haze is reached after short exposure times, even less than 90 days.
In these areas, a much higher cleaning frequency seems necessary. A
greater frequency of maintenance and cleaning implies higher costs as
well as further possible damage of the glass artefacts resulting from
cleaning operations.
PM10 seems to be the main responsible for glass soiling, contributing
signiﬁcantly over central and southern Europe, with peaks located in
northern Italy, southern Spain, western Turkey and some parts of the
Russian Federation. NO 2 also plays an important role in contributing
to glass soiling, but its action seems to be more localized in some
areas of northern Italy, France, Germany, Holland, the Netherlands and
the Russian Federation. Finally, SO 2 plays a negligible role in almost
the entire domain, with the exception of some areas generally located
in Germany, Poland, the Balkans, Turkey, Romania, Hungary, and the
Russian Federation (Supplemental material, Fig. S7).
3.8. Susceptibility of UNESCO World Cultural Heritage sites
Fig. 9a shows, in descending order, the surface recession rates for
Portland limestone predicted at the 1276 cells of the studied domain
that house properties listed in the WHL. The predicted recession rates,
ﬁrst year exposure, appear to be quite contained and sometimes close
to the background value (3.2 μm). However, in 109 cells the recession
rate exceeds the target suggested by ICP Materials for protecting
infrastructure materials and cultural heritage monuments for the year
2050 (6.4 μm, ﬁrst year exposure) and in 16 cases exceeds the target
set for 2020 (8.0 μm). For sandstone ( Fig. 9 b), the recession rate for
this material exceeds the 2050 target (5.5μm) in 31 cells and the target
for 2020 (7.0 μm) in 16 cells. The general lower rate of surface recession
for sandstone artefacts is attributable to today's low levels of atmo-
spheric SO2. In the European Union (EU-28), SO x emissions decreased
by 90% from 1990 to 2017 as a result of a wide range of environmental
policy measures and the entry into force of stricter emission standards.
This reduction in emissions had a corresponding impact on air quality.
The effect of reduced SO2 air concentrations in the estimate of the cur-
rent rate of recession appears more marked for the sandstone since
only for this material the SO 2-dominating dose-response function was
used.
Overall, the corrosion rate of copper ( Fig. 9c) appears to be high in
vast areas of the studied domain. In 871 cells out of 1276 identi ﬁed as
hosting UNESCO cultural heritage sites, the corrosion rate of copper
was estimated to be greater than the 2050 target (0.64 μm) and in
165 cells higher than the 2020 target (0.8μm). The risk for bronze arte-
facts (Fig. 9d) seems much more limited. Only in 12 cells of the studied
domain where UNESCO sites are present, the corrosion rate of the
bronze exceeds the target of 0.5 μm, ﬁrst year exposure, set for 2050
and in only 6 the target for 2020 (0.6 μm) is exceeded. Regarding steel
(Fig. 9 e), in a small number of cells (33) the corrosion rate exceeds
the 2050 target of 16 μm and in 11 exceeds the target for 2020 of
20 μm. Zinc is another metal that seems particularly at risk of corrosion
in large areas. The corrosion rate of zinc ( Fig. 9f) was calculated to be
greater than 0.9 μm (2050 target) in 412 cells out of 1276 identi ﬁed as
hosting UNESCO cultural heritage sites and it was greater than 1.1 μm
(2020 target) in 62 cells of the studied domain.
These results contrast with what was reported by Di Turo et al.
(2016) which, starting from air pollution data for the years 1980,
1990, 2000 and 2010 provided by the EMEP model at a resolution of
50 × 50 km and downscaled to a resolution of 28 × 28 km, found that

Although the sites in Table 3 are shown in descending order accord-
ing to the number of materials at risk and the predicted level of damage
for each material, their order should not be interpreted as a ranking of
the magnitude of the threats and the importance of their impact on
the property. Indeed, it should be interpreted as a list of sites where
the potential to have detrimental effects on the materials of cultural
heritage due to atmospheric pollution is higher. No veriﬁcation was car-
ried out to ascertain an imminent danger and the actual presence of all
materials in the sites included in this list has not been veri ﬁed. Never-
theless, it is recognized that the damage of air pollution is not limited
to materials for which a dose-response function has been de ﬁned and
that all materials suffer damage from the combined action of atmo-
spheric parameters and pollution. In addition, it is known that ﬂuctua-
tions in climate such as frost-thaw cycles and drying and wetting
episodes have physical effects that degrade building stone ( Sabbioni
et al., 2010). For coastal sites some additional effect would be expected
due to chloride from sea salt aerosol deposition ( Grøntoft and
Svenningsen, 2009) or chloride deposition from road salting. Such ef-
fects are not included in the applied dose-response functions. The gen-
eralization of the present study can serve as a basis for stimulating
additional studies and site-speci ﬁc analyzes, as well as highlighting
the need for further measures and policies for atmospheric pollution re-
duction to prevent further damage.
An analysis of the environment surrounding the sites listed in
Table 3 was performed to help clarify and explain the main factors de-
termining the local levels of atmospheric pollution and therefore the
predicted damage of the materials from which these heritage properties
are made. The analysis was performed by examining the information
available on the European Pollutant Release and Transfer Register (E-
PRTR) website ( http://prtr.ec.europa.eu/FacilityLevels.aspx ) and the
air pollution website of the European Environment Agency ( https://
www.eea.europa.eu/themes/air/explore-air-pollution-data ). The E –
PRTR is the most comprehensive and readily accessible register for in-
dustrial emissions on an EU scale. The EEA database provides available
data and information from Europe's air quality monitoring network.
Most of the UNESCO properties listed inTable 3 as potentially at risk
are located in urban, densely populated areas. Although pollution levels
have dropped in most European cities, motor vehicle trafﬁc is still one of
the most important causes of air pollution in urban environments (EEA,
2019). Biomass burning (residential heating and cooking on woodﬁres)
is a problematic local issue as it contributes considerably to PM emis-
sions (EEA, 2018). For instance, domestic heating has been reported as
an issue in Antwerp ( Nagl et al., 2018 ), Istanbul ( Nur Kara, 2018 ),
Kraków ( Kaczmarczyk et al., 2020 ), Athens ( Gratsea et al., 2017 ),
North Italy (Perrino et al., 2014), Venice (Benetello et al., 2017), and Na-
ples (Sirignano et al., 2019). Agriculture is the main source of NH3 emis-
sions. Ammonia emissions are important because NH3 is responsible for
neutralizing a large fraction of acidic gases producing ammonium sul-
phate ((NH4)2SO4) and ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3), thus promoting
the formation of secondary atmospheric particles (Viana et al., 2016).
In addition to vehicular traf ﬁc, environmental stressors in many of
the cities that host the UNESCO sites listed in Table 3 derive from the
presence of port activities for trade, freight and cruise ships. The marine
transport sector contributes signi ﬁcantly to air pollution, especially
along the coastal areas near busy shipping routes ( Corbett et al., 2007;
EEA, 2013; APICE, 2013; Transport and Environment, 2019). Emissions
are also generated in seaports and come from a variety of sources:
ships calling in a port, loading and unloading of goods, storing and
warehousing, transport from the port with its hinterland and the indus-
try located within the port area. Important port cities that are home to
the UNESCO sites listed inTable 3are St. Petersburg, Antwerp, Hamburg,

Air pollution, particularly in urban areas, is a concern for its negative effects on the materials of the built environ-
ment. Cities are also home to a large part of our cultural heritage. Air pollution accelerates the natural processes of
deterioration of the materials of historic buildings and monuments, causing premature aging and reducing their
aesthetic value. The present paper aims to assess the current potential damage due to air pollution on different
materials through Europe. Several corrosion and soiling maps were produced by applying widely used dose-
response functions. One of the priorities of this study was to provide an estimate of the effects of air pollution
on UNESCO World Heritage cultural sites throughout Europe. The potential risk for cultural heritage monuments
was estimated on the basis of exceeding tolerable degradation thresholds suggested for each material. The results
show that, despite the signiﬁcant improvements in air quality in Europe over the past few decades, air pollution is
still considerable and continues to be an important agent of degradation of cultural heritage, particularly in
anthropized areas. Although the methodology used in this study provides a simpliﬁed assessment of the likeli-
hood of damage to UNESCO's cultural heritage in Europe from air pollution, it provides a unique perspective
and the potential risk is assessed on a common basis. The results obtained contribute to a better understanding
of the existing risk deriving from atmospheric pollution and to highlighting those sites, generally located in areas
where anthropogenic activity is relevant, that need particular attention. The present paper can serve as a basis for
stimulating additional studies and site-speciﬁc analyzes, as well as highlighting the need for further measures
and policies for atmospheric pollution reduction in cities and in the surroundings of sensitive historic buildings
and monuments to prevent further damage.

This discrepancy can be attributed to several factors. First of all, Di
Turo et al. considered only the targets set for 2020 ( n = 2.5) and not
the targets for 2050 (n = 2). Moreover, in their selection of UNESCO
sites they neglected the presence of serial and transboundary sites,
thus signiﬁcantly reducing the number of locations that hosts UNESCO
World Cultural Heritage. Finally, their assessments were made with a
coarser spatial resolution, 28 × 28 km, and this could have in ﬂuenced
the estimated concentration of air pollutants, smoothed into a larger
grid cell, and therefore would have led to underestimating the degrada-
tion rates of the materials.
Reference levels for the soiling of modern glass in the background at-
mosphere and targets for protecting this material from soiling are not
suggested by ICP Materials. However, in 920 out of the 1276 cells of
the studied domain hosting UNESCO properties 1% haze is reached
after less than one year and in 199 cells this haze level is reached after
less than six months.
Table 3 shows the cells of the studied domain hosting properties
listed in the WHL where the recession rates of stone materials and the
corrosion rates of the metallic materials appears to be higher according
to the following criterion: at least three of the degradation rates are
higher than the targets suggested by ICP Materials for 2050 and, of
these, at least one is greater than the targets suggested for 2020. For
each cell in the domain, the UNESCO world cultural site that is housed
in the cell is also reported. According to this choice, some UNESCO
sites that could be at risk of damage from air pollution, due for example
to exceeding a target for a single material for that site, may not have
been included in the table.
According to UNESCO (https://whc.unesco.org/en/factors/), air pol-
lution is one of the threats/factors affecting the Outstanding Universal
Value (OUV) of World Heritage properties. In the second cycle of the Pe-
riodic Reporting Exercise for the Europe Region (UNESCO, 2015)6 5o u t
